newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope starts seeing aides, takes solid food.
newsitem.headline: Pope starts seeing aides, takes solid food.

text.p: Pope John Paul held brief meetings with close aides on Friday, a sign he is eager to get back to work just three days after surgery to remove his appendix, and doctors said he was making a "brilliant" recovery.

"He slept well, he took solid food this morning, his intestinal functions are going well, his temperature is normal," Professor Corrado Manni, the Gemelli hospital's chief aneasthetist, told Reuters after visiting the Pope.
"He is making a brilliant recovery. He smiles all the time," Manni added. "I didn't think that he would have such a swift and good post-operative recovery."
An official medical bulletin said the 76-year-old Pope, who is expected to leave hospital early next week, continued to show no sign of a fever or abdominal pain.

"The Holy Father has taken several walks along the corridor outside his room. He has dedicated himself at length to prayer and reading and has granted brief audiences to his direct associates," the bulletin said.

The Polish-born Pope had a 50-minute operation at the Gemelli on Tuesday to remove an inflamed appendix. Doctors said biopsies showed that there was no trace of any recurrence of a colon tumour removed in 1992.
Vatican officials have said the Pope plans to celebrate his first public mass at the Vatican to mark a religious anniversary on October 27 but would probably resume short audiences earlier.
He marks the 18th anniversary of his 1978 election next Wednesday.
The Pope is keen to be in good form by November 1, when he will celebrate the 50th anniversary of his ordination as a priest. He has invited all priests ordained in 1946 to come to Rome.
Although doctors have suggested to the Pope that he slow down, the Pontiff has four trips planned for next year, including a visit to his native Poland.
Vatican prelates say that despite his physical fraility and advancing years, the Pope is unlikely to ease up.
"This isn't the first time the question has come up," Cardinal Paul Poupard, a French member of the Curia who was on the Pope's trip to France last month, told Corriere della Sera newspaper.
"He thanks the cardinals or the surgeons who tell him to rest, sends them away with a friendly smile and then does what he has to do," Poupard said.
